explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Peter says there were false prophets among the people back then, “…just as there will be false teachers among you.” (2 Peter 2:1) Same kind of trouble, new faces. And these ones don't come with a warning label.

Kings are a fair guess, since Israel had plenty of them. But Peter's warning here isn't about anybody on a throne. He says “…there will be false teachers among you.” (2 Peter 2:1) The trouble is right in the room with the believers, not off in a palace.

Armies marching in is trouble you can see coming from a mile away. Peter's warning is quieter than that. He says “…there will be false teachers among you.” (2 Peter 2:1) Nobody blows a trumpet for someone who just walks in and starts talking.

Peter says the opposite, friend. He says these teachers “…will secretly introduce destructive heresies…” (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly means no parade and no announcement. If heresies wore name tags, this would be a whole lot easier.

That's right. Peter says they “…will secretly introduce destructive heresies…” (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly means nobody sees it coming, with no sign and no trumpet. That's why Peter warns the believers ahead of time.
Yes, baker. Peter says they go so far as “…even denying the Master who bought them…” (2 Peter 2:1). That's not a small slip. It's turning away from the very Master who bought them.
I see why you'd think so, since Peter just mentioned false prophets. But the one they deny is the Master who bought them. Peter says it plainly in 2 Peter 2:1. The prophets aren't who he names there.

Elders are good folks to have around, but Peter doesn't mention them in this passage. He says the false teachers are “…even denying the Master who bought them…” (2 Peter 2:1). That's who they deny. Anyone can nod along with the elders, but this goes much further.
Peter says the opposite. He says “Many will follow in their depravity…” (2 Peter 2:2). Many, not a handful. A handful is a small group chat, and Peter is describing a big one.
That's right, friend. Peter says “Many will follow in their depravity…” (2 Peter 2:2). That's a crowd, not a handful. It's a good reason he's warning them now.
Yes, baker. Peter says “…the way of truth will be defamed.” (2 Peter 2:2). Defamed means its name gets dragged around unfairly. And he says it happens because of the many who follow these teachers.
Peace is a lovely word, but it isn't the one Peter wrote. He says “…the way of truth will be defamed.” (2 Peter 2:2). It's truth that takes the hit. Peace didn't even make it into that verse.

Wisdom sounds right, and it's a good thing to want. But Peter's word is truth. He says “…the way of truth will be defamed.” (2 Peter 2:2). That's what gets dragged around because of the false teachers.

That's it. Peter says “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” (2 Peter 2:3) Greed is when someone eyes the whole cookie box and wants your share too. And the tool they use is words that sound good but deceive.

Fear is a fair guess, since fear makes people do all kinds of things. But Peter names something else. He says “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” (2 Peter 2:3) Greed is the word he picked.

Grief is a heavy word, and Peter doesn't use it here. He says “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” (2 Peter 2:3) Greed is what drives their exploiting. The deceptive words are how they go about it.

explanations.answer: Cast them into hell in chains of darkness
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Peter says God “…cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2 Peter 2:4). He did not spare the angels when they sinned. That's Exhibit A in Peter's case.

explanations.answer: Sent them out to wander the earth in exile
explanations.explanation: Wandering free sounds almost gentle next to what Peter says. He says God cast them into hell and placed them “…in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2 Peter 2:4). Chains mean they're held, not roaming. Nothing in the verse sends them wandering.

explanations.answer: Set them to guard the way to Eden's tree
explanations.explanation: Guarding the way to the tree of life is a real Bible job, but it's a different scene. Genesis 3:24 mentions cherubim stationed there. Peter's verse is about angels who sinned, and God placed them “…in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2 Peter 2:4).

That's him, baker. Peter says God “…preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight” (2 Peter 2:5). Eight people were preserved, and Noah was one of them. Even in Exhibit B, God knew exactly who to keep.

Enoch is a good name to think of. Genesis 5:24 says he walked with God and then God took him. But Peter's verse is about the flood and the eight, and the name he gives is Noah, “a preacher of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5).

Abraham, the man God told to leave his homeland (Genesis 12:1), is a big name, but he isn't in this verse. Peter is talking about the flood on the ungodly. The one preserved among the eight is Noah, “a preacher of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5).

explanations.answer: As an example of what is coming on the ungodly
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter says God condemned Sodom and Gomorrah, “…reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6). It's Exhibit C, and Peter says what it's an example of. He doesn't add any other reason.

explanations.answer: As a warning to the king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt had plenty of kings, but none of them show up in Peter's verse. He says God reduced the cities to ashes “…as an example of what is coming on the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6). That's the purpose he gives. Peter never says who was meant to see it.

explanations.answer: To make room for the tribes of Israel
explanations.explanation: Peter never mentions Israel's tribes in this verse. He says God reduced the cities to ashes “…as an example of what is coming on the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6). That's the reason on the page, and I'm not going to bake in anything extra.

That's right, baker. Peter says Lot, the righteous man God rescued, “…was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard” (2 Peter 2:8). He lived among them day after day. I think that sounds exhausting, and Peter calls it torment.

Peter actually says it outright. Lot, the righteous man God rescued, lived among them day after day and “…was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard” (2 Peter 2:8). I think that's a heavy way to live. He was righteous and he saw it all.

explanations.answer: Rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for punishment
explanations.explanation: That's the whole point of the ifs. Peter says “…the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.” (2 Peter 2:9) Noah and Lot were the rescued ones. The angels, the ancient world and the cities were the held ones.

explanations.answer: Keep the godly from ever facing any trials
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't promise that. He says the Lord knows how to “…rescue the godly from trials…” (2 Peter 2:9). Lot's own story shows he lived among lawless people day after day before the rescue (2 Peter 2:8). Rescued from trials, friend, not kept from ever meeting them.

explanations.answer: Spare the unrighteous if a few godly remain
explanations.explanation: Peter's examples don't go that way. God preserved Noah and the eight, but He did not spare the ancient world (2 Peter 2:5). Peter says the Lord knows how to “…hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.” (2 Peter 2:9) The godly get rescued, and the unrighteous don't get a pass because of them.

Peter says the opposite. He says “Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.” (2 Peter 2:10) Timid is not in that description. Bold, self-willed and unafraid, that's the picture.

That's right. Peter says “Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.” (2 Peter 2:10) No tiptoeing, no second thoughts. Bold is the word, baker, and it's not a compliment here.

explanations.answer: They don't dare bring such slanderous charges
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Peter says “Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.” (2 Peter 2:11) So even the stronger ones hold back. The false teachers don't, and that's Peter's whole point.

explanations.answer: They bring even harsher charges of their own
explanations.explanation: That would be the opposite of what Peter says. He says the angels are “greater in strength and power,” and yet they don't “dare to bring such slanderous charges” (2 Peter 2:11). They hold back, even though they're stronger. The false teachers charge ahead.

explanations.answer: They take the false teachers' side
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't put the angels on the false teachers' side at all. He says that “not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges” (2 Peter 2:11). They show restraint before the Lord. The false teachers show none.
That's it. Peter says “They blaspheme in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). Think of someone giving you stamping advice who has never held a stamper. I've met that guy, and he was LOUD.
Peter says the opposite. He says they blaspheme “…in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). Years of study would mean they understood. Peter says they don't.

Angels are actually the ones who hold back in the verse before this one. Peter says they don't dare bring such slanderous charges (2 Peter 2:11). The false teachers blaspheme “…in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). They didn't get it from the angels.

Peter says it the other way around. He says “They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight.” (2 Peter 2:13) Broad daylight means no waiting for dark and no hiding. They're comfortable doing it in the open.
That's right, friend. Peter says “They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight.” (2 Peter 2:13) Broad daylight, not after dark. They don't even bother to hide it.

explanations.answer: As they feast with the believers
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Peter says they are “blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) They sit right at the table with the believers. That's close enough to pass the cookie box.

explanations.answer: As they pray with the believers
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't say prayer. He says they are “…reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) The setting is a feast. Prayer isn't mentioned in the verse.

explanations.answer: As they sing with the believers
explanations.explanation: Singing is a good guess for a gathering, but it isn't what Peter wrote. He says they are “…reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) The word is feast. Nobody's holding a songbook in that verse.
That's right. Peter says “…they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Unstable means not steady, like a cooling rack with one short leg. It's the shaky ones who get pulled along.
The wise aren't who Peter names. He says “…they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Unstable is the word he picked. Nothing in the verse says the wise get seduced.

Peter does talk about greed, so wealth makes sense as a guess. But he says “…they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Their target is the unstable, not the wealthy. The verse says nothing about money in the people they seduce.

Yes, friend. Peter says they follow “…the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) Balaam is the prophet from the story in Numbers 22. The love of that payment is the way Peter says the false teachers follow.

Praise is a fair guess for a prophet, but it isn't what Peter says. He says Balaam “…loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) It's the wages that he loved. Peter says nothing about praise in the verse.

That's a quiet, lovely thing to love, but Peter names something else. He says Balaam “…loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) Wages are what the false teachers are following. The wilderness doesn't come up.

That's right! Peter says Balaam “…was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice…” (2 Peter 2:16). I've been corrected by a kitchen timer before. A donkey is next level.

Ravens do turn up in Elijah's story, Elijah being a prophet of Israel (1 Kings 17:6), but not here. Peter says Balaam “…was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey…” (2 Peter 2:16). A donkey was the one who did the rebuking. A raven stays out of this one.

Lions have their own Bible moments, like in Daniel's story (Daniel 6:16). Daniel was an exile in Babylon who was thrown into a lion's den. But Peter says Balaam “…was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey…” (2 Peter 2:16). No lion in this one, baker.

Yes, baker. Peter says “Blackest darkness is reserved for them.” (2 Peter 2:17) That's a heavy line, and I'll let it be heavy. It comes right after he calls them springs without water and mists driven by a storm.

Peter actually says it directly. He writes “Blackest darkness is reserved for them.” (2 Peter 2:17) It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up. It follows his picture of them as springs without water and mists driven by a storm.

explanations.answer: Those just escaping people who live in error
explanations.explanation: That's it. Peter says they “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) These are people who are just getting out. The false teachers go after them.

explanations.answer: Those who have walked with Jesus for years
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't say that. He says the false teachers “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) The word is just escaping, so these are people at the start of getting out. Years of walking aren't in the verse.

explanations.answer: Those who have never heard of Jesus at all
explanations.explanation: Peter's target is different. He says they “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) They're already on their way out of error. That's the group the false teachers go after.

Yes, baker. Peter says “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) That's like a guy selling you a map while he's lost himself. Freedom is the pitch, but they're not free.

Strangers to depravity would be the opposite of what Peter says. He writes “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) They're not strangers to it. They're slaves.

Rulers would make the freedom pitch sound pretty convincing. But Peter says “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) They don't rule over it. It rules over them.
Peter says the opposite, friend. He says “For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.” (2 Peter 2:19) Whatever has mastered you is what you're a slave to. Freedom isn't automatic.

That's right. Peter says “For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.” (2 Peter 2:19) So the freedom the false teachers promise doesn't hold up. They're slaves themselves, and they're handing out freedom.

explanations.answer: It is worse than it was at first
explanations.explanation: That's what Peter says. If they escape and then get entangled again, “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) It's a sad turn. He wants the believers to see it clearly.

explanations.answer: It is the same as it was before
explanations.explanation: Same as before sounds fair, but Peter says more. He says “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) Worse, not the same. Going back costs more than staying put.

explanations.answer: It is better for having escaped once
explanations.explanation: I'd like that to be true, but Peter says the opposite. He writes “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) Escaping and then getting entangled again leaves them worse off. Peter doesn't give them credit for the first escape.

Yes, baker. Peter says “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.” (2 Peter 2:21) That's a serious line. Knowing the way and then turning from it is what he's talking about.

Peter says exactly that, friend. He writes “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.” (2 Peter 2:21) It's a serious thing to know the way and then turn from it. That's the point of the verse.

explanations.answer: Going back to the mess they escaped
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. A dog returns to its vomit, and a sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud (2 Peter 2:22). Both of them leave, and both of them go right back. A washed sow stays clean about as long as my apron does around cookie dough.

explanations.answer: Never leaving the mess in the first place
explanations.explanation: The proverbs say something different. A dog returns, and a sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud (2 Peter 2:22). Returning and going back mean they had left. The picture is of leaving and then returning.

explanations.answer: Cleaning up and staying clean for good
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of Peter's picture. The sow in his proverb is washed, but then she “goes back to her wallowing in the mud.” (2 Peter 2:22) The dog “returns” too. Neither of them stays clean.
